title: Common Risk Factors in the Returns on Stocks, Bonds (and Options), Redux

p.t: Finance theory predicts a tight connection between the major types of corporate securities, such as stocks, corporate bonds, and options (see, e.g., Black and Scholes, 1973;Merton, 1974). Existence of a pervasive factor structure suggests that cross-sectional variation in expected returns should reflect the different exposures of individual assets to common sources of risk, which cannot be diversified away (see, e.g., Ross, 1976). Yet empirical challenges have impeded efforts to identify common factors across different markets. For instance, available datasets covering asset classes with short maturities, such as corporate bonds and options, have far more securities than time-series observations, making estimation of factors via principal components infeasible. Popular approaches, such as the portfolio-sorting of Fama and French (1992), also struggle to construct factors in the face of a large set of characteristics that are known to forecast returns within each asset class (Cochrane, 2011). 1In this paper, we pursue a new approach to extracting latent factors directly from the large cross sections of individual securities of the three asset markets based on the regressed-PCA method in Chen, Roussanov, and Wang (2021). The key advantage of this approach is that it works effectively on unbalanced panels of assets with large cross-sections but short time series of individual asset returns. Regressed-PCA combines standard building blocks-Fama-MacBeth cross-sectional regressions (Fama and MacBeth, 1973) and principal component analysis (PCA)-in a semiparametric conditional factor model, with time-varying factor loadings and pricing errors of individual asset returns modeled as flexible functions of observable characteristics. Essentially, regressed-PCA transforms a high-dimensional, unbalanced panel of individual assets into a smaller balanced panel of characteristic-managed portfolios and then applies standard PCA to these portfolios to uncover the latent factors. Chen, Roussanov, and Wang (2021) show that the regressed-PCA estimators have desirable large-N asymptotic properties despite short time-series, making the approach particularly well-suited for identifying common factors across multiple asset classes.

Our empirical analysis is based on monthly observations from July 2004 to December 2021 for stocks, corporate bonds, and options from over 8,000 firms. Our estimates reveal a strong and systematic common factor structure across the corporate asset classes. First, the common factors are closely related to well-established observable risk factors in the stock, corporate bond, and option markets, but cannot be fully explained by these observed factors. Second, the common factors significantly load on all asset classes rather than being tied to any single market. This is also confirmed by an analysis based on a decomposition of the factors into asset-class-specific components. Third, the common factors are closely related to key macro-financial variables, exhibiting both strong contemporaneous correlations with and demonstrating predictive power for variables such as aggregate consumption and inflation, economic uncertainty, intermediary capital ratios, monetary policy and credit conditions, as well as other real economic indicators. Most of the factors carry substantial risk premia, with several of the leading ten factors achieving Sharpe ratios in excess of one in-sample (and some exceeding 2 out-of-sample). Common factors also display substantial in-sample and out-of-sample explanatory power for both time-series and cross-sectional variation in asset returns across the three asset classes. Top ten common factors explain around 67% of in-sample return variation in the managed portfolios, and 16.76% of in-sample (5.42% of out-of-sample) individual asset return variation, pooled across the three markets. The explanatory power of common factors in the three asset classes is comparable, although their out-of-sample fit in options is relatively weak. All of these findings are consistent with a fairly strong common factor structure across markets.

However, common factors do not fully span the cross-section of expected asset returns, in that a number of asset characteristics have statistically significant explanatory power for average returns above and beyond their contribution to time-varying factor loadings, implying non-zero pricing errors. Motivated by this evidence, we construct a pure-alpha "arbitrage" portfolio that exploits the predictive power of characteristics while bearing zero exposure to the common factors. The pure-alpha strategy generates a substantial out-of-sample Sharpe ratio (around 2, depending on the number of factors being hedged out); and its decomposition into asset-class-specific components indicates that the high Sharpe ratio comes primarily from the option component, reflecting the large mispricing in options, with some of the equity managed portfolios also contributing significantly, while bond portfolios less so. We apply our model estimation approach to constructing mean-variance efficient (MVE) portfolios of individual assets across all three markets jointly. Assuming that idiosyncratic errors are homoskedastic in the conditional factor model, MVE portfolio can be approximated with the characteristic-managed portfolios. In turn, for the covariance matrix estimation of the managed portfolios, the dimensionality can be further reduced by taking advantage of the common factor structure, even without assuming factor pricing. The joint MVE portfolio delivers high Sharpe ratios both in-sample and out-of-sample, significantly exceeding those of MVE portfolios in each single market, with the highest out-of-sample annualized Sharpe ratios around 3. We analyze the properties of the joint MVE portfolio by decomposing it into asset-class-specific components. Our findings indicate that much of its superior performance is due to mutual hedging among these components, which is further attributed to their opposite loadings on the same common factors. We find that asset-class-specific components hedge against common factors such that the joint MVE portfolio bears almost zero exposures to most of the factors, even those earning positive Sharpe ratios.

Finally, we measure the extent of integration (or segmentation) between different asset markets based on common factors. Building on the framework of Chen and Knez (1995), we construct a formal statistical test for the degree of market segmentation or "market distance," which is measured using the estimated difference in risk premia of the common basis payoffs between two asset classes. Conveniently, a set of common factors extracted jointly from individual assets across markets serves as a natural empirical proxy for the orthogonal basis of the common payoff space. We further demonstrate that this market distance can be equivalently measured by the difference in the prices of common payoffs in the corresponding markets, which reflects their relative mispricing. Our empirical results show a statistically significant degree of market segmentation for all market pairs. In particular, we show that the option market is largely segmented from the other two markets, while equity and corporate bond markets are somewhat less segmented from one another. These findings point to the potential limits to arbitrage across different markets. We further demonstrate that market segmentation helps to account for the cross-market hedging that emerges among the asset-class-specific components of the joint MVE portfolios, as it optimally exploits differences in the observed factor risk premia across markets. Our paper contributes to a voluminous empirical asset pricing literature that studies the cross-section of multiple asset classes. Extensive research has documented predictive linkages between stocks and corporate bonds (see, e.g., Gebhardt, Hvidkjaer, and Swaminathan, 2005;Chordia, Goyal, Nozawa, Subrahmanyam, and Tong, 2017;Bali, Goyal, Huang, Jiang, and Wen, 2022;Dickerson, Julliard, and Mueller, 2026), stocks and options (see, e.g., Bali and Hovakimian, 2009;Johnson and So, 2012;Cao and Han, 2013;Christoffersen, Goyenko, Jacobs, and Karoui, 2018;Bali, Beckmeyer, Moerke, and Weigert, 2021;Goyenko and Zhang, 2021), and corporate bonds and options (see, e.g., Culp, Nozawa, and Veronesi, 2018;Cao, Goyal, Xiao, and Zhan, 2023). Beyond these bilateral linkages, studies such as Asness, Moskowitz, and Pedersen (2013), He, Kelly, and Manela (2017), and Lettau, Maggiori, and Weber (2014) propose unified macro-finance factors that price assets jointly across various asset classes. A closely related work by Bali, Beckmeyer, and Goyal (2023) extends the Instrumented Principal Component Analysis (IPCA) in Kelly, Pruitt, and Su (2019) to estimate a joint factor model for the same three asset classes. We extract common factors via regressed-PCA, which, unlike other methods used in the literature, accommodates nonlinearity and explicitly accounts for pricing errors, as well as permits formal statistical inference. We enrich the literature with a set of common factors across the three markets and pairwise factors for different market pairs. More importantly, we use common factors to construct joint MVE portfolios spanning the three asset classes and to develop a measure of segmentation between them.

Our paper adds to the growing asset pricing literature on factor models for corporate bonds and options. These two asset markets are relatively under-studied compared to the stock market, though recent work has begun to explore factor structures specific to these two markets. For corporate bonds, Kelly, Palhares, and Pruitt (2023) apply IPCA to extract five latent factors in bond returns, while others identify several aggregate risks such as liquidity (see, e.g., Lin, Wang, and Wu, 2011), long-run consumption risk (see, e.g., Elkamhi, Jo, and Nozawa, 2024), and institutional constraints (see, e.g., Bali, Subrahmanyam, and Wen, 2021). For options, in addition to the traditional parametric models (see, e.g., Duffie, Pan, and Singleton, 2000), the research on factor-based explanations has grown rapidly. Büchner and Kelly (2022) and Goyal and Saretto (2025) use IPCA to study the factor structure of index options and equity options, respectively; Horenstein, Vasquez, and Xiao (2026) use PCA to extract latent factors from option portfolios. Similarly, Christoffersen, Fournier, and Jacobs (2018) extract factors from the implied volatility surface to explain the cross-section of option prices, and Karakaya (2013) suggests a three-factor model (level, slope, value) for delta-hedged returns. Others focus on specific characteristics such as embedded leverage and volatility deviation (see, e.g., Frazzini and Pedersen, 2022;Goyal and Saretto, 2009;Zhan, Han, Cao, and Tong, 2022). In this paper, we also extract the factors in each asset class based on regressed-PCA, providing additional sets of corporate bond and option factors to the literature.

We develop a new framework to construct the joint MVE portfolio from individual assets across markets. For multiple asset classes, the cross section of assets is much larger than their time-series dimension, and the resulting panels are usually unbalanced. Existing approaches (see, e.g., Ledoit and Wolf, 2017), which focus on the estimation of the highdimensional covariance matrix, are not feasible in this context. Based on the conditional factor model, our approach incorporates characteristics and enhances the approximation of the conditional MVE portfolio, and further translates the covariance matrix estimation for a high-dimensional unbalanced panel into the estimation for a low-dimensional set of common factors. Consequently, the construction of a joint MVE portfolio across markets becomes feasible with common factors. We also propose a formal measure of market segmentation, building on the conceptual framework of Chen and Knez (1995). We demonstrate that the extent of market segmentation should be reflected by the difference in risk premia associated with the same common factors in different markets, which is conceptually similar to recent studies (see, e.g., Choi and Kim, 2018;Sandulescu, 2019;Patton and Weller, 2022). We highlight the natural role of our common factors as benchmark basis payoffs across markets, and develop several formal statistical tests of market integration (or segmentation). Our rigorous quantification of segmentation also aligns with the findings on the cross-market limits to arbitrage as in Kapadia and Pu (2012), Greenwood, Hanson, and Liao (2018), Siriwardane, Sunderam, and Wallen (2025), Wittwer and Uthemann (2025), and Chen, Chen, and Li (2026). Our empirical evidence could potentially provide helpful guidance to theoretical models on crossmarket arbitrage by focusing attention on the relative mispricing of common factors across markets, rather than idiosyncratic risk or the degree of time-series comovement.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the regressed-PCA procedure in a conditional factor model across markets. Section 3 describes the data. Section 4 examines the cross-market commonality captured by factors and their economic relevance. Section 5 presents the in-sample and out-of-sample performance of the common factor model. Section 6 constructs the joint MVE portfolios across markets using common factors. Section 7 measures market segmentation based on common factors. Section 8 concludes.

The model in (2.5) with common factor structure is estimated using an analogous twostep procedure. The Fama-MacBeth cross-sectional regression (R t on Z t´1 ) yields tradable characteristic-managed portfolios in different asset markets. Notably, this step is equivalent to running separate cross-sectional regressions within each asset class, enabling us to incorporate both security-specific and firm-level characteristics (like firm's leverage) in different asset classes. We then extract the common factors (F C ) by applying PCA to the pooled managed portfolios of all asset classes. The resulting factors are zero-cost tradable portfolios constructed on the managed portfolios with weights p B. Two properties of the regressed-PCA approach established by Chen, Roussanov, and Wang (2021) are crucial in our setting. First, the method has large-N asymptotic properties and does not require large T . This is particularly appealing in settings with a vast number of cross-sectional observations but relatively short sample periods (N " T ). As shown in Section 3, we observe only 210 monthly periods but more than 5,000 individual assets each month. Second, regressed-PCA accommodates unbalanced panels. By performing the period-by-period Fama-MacBeth regressions, the method transforms unbalanced, high-dimensional individual asset returns into a balanced, low-dimensional set of tradable managed portfolios. This property is particularly important for options, where individual contracts have short maturities. In addition to these useful properties, regressed-PCA provides formal tests of hypotheses such as αp¨q " 0 and βp¨q " 0 using a weighted bootstrap procedure developed by Chen, Roussanov, and Wang (2021).

The monthly data on stock returns and characteristics are from Freyberger, Neuhierl, and Weber (2020) and Freyberger, Höppner, Neuhierl, and Weber (2025) until December 2021. We choose 35 available characteristics, with more details listed in Appendix A1.

The monthly corporate bond returns and characteristics are from the dataset in Dicker- son, Robotti, and Rossetti (2023), which are sourced from the WRDS bond database and Mergent's FISD. The dataset accounts for market microstructure noise by employing the adjustment procedure proposed by Andreani, Palhares, and Richardson (2024), which significantly reduces return volatility for illiquid bonds and also reconciles returns derived from transaction data with those from institutional-grade quote data. We further supplement this dataset with Mergent's FISD for contract-level details such as coupon rates, convertible terms, and issuer information. The resulting datasets are then merged with firm-level characteristics from Compustat and CRSP. The monthly individual corporate bond returns are computed using representative price (P ), accrued interest (AI), and coupons (cpn) on each end-of-month date. We select monthend prices due to the illiquidity and infrequent trading in corporate bond markets, aiming to balance the trade-off between sample size and the use of potentially stale price data. Specifically, for each corporate bond on each month-end date, we select the price if it is available within 5 calendar days before the month-end; otherwise, we mark the price as missing. We compute the accrued interest over the fractional period between the last coupon payment date and the month-end date. The monthly bond return is then calculated as We choose 26 characteristics that are informative for corporate bond returns, as documented by the literature (see, e.g., Kelly, Palhares, and Pruitt, 2023;Bao, Pan, and Wang, 2011). Among these, there are 12 characteristics related to bond contracts, including bond age (age), coupon (cpn), rating (rating), issue amount (issue size), duration (duration), spread (CS), bond momentum (bond mom), spread momentum (spread mom), value-atrisk (V aR), bond short-term reversal (bond rev), bond long-term reversal (bond ltrev), and illiquidity (illiq). We also include 14 firm-level characteristics, which are also used in the analysis of stock returns. These are idiosyncratic volatility (idiovol), momentum (mom), book leverage (lev), operating leverage (ol), earnings-to-price ratio (e2p), tangibility (tan), total debt (debt), debt-to-EBITDA (d2ebitda), distance-to-default (DD), and five characteristics related to Fama-French factors (beta, prof , mktcap, invest, bm). Appendix A1 presents the sources and detailed description of these characteristics.

The monthly data on individual equity option returns and characteristics are from Option-Metrics. We obtain underlying stock information such as returns, prices, share codes, and trading volume from CRSP. Importantly, to avoid recording errors and distortions caused by extremely illiquid options, we apply standard data filters commonly used in the literature. 5All filters are applied properly to avoid look-ahead bias, where Appendix A1 provides all the details. Outliers in the options data can significantly distort the estimation, especially during periods of extreme financial market turmoil. To mitigate this issue, we trim the options data by excluding returns below the 1st percentile and above the 99th percentile in each period. The trimmed sample is used only for in-sample estimation, while we retain the untrimmed data in the out-of-sample analysis to avoid look-ahead bias. We focus on call options, which are more actively traded than puts (see, e.g., Zhan, Han, Cao, and Tong, 2022;Christoffersen, Goyenko, Jacobs, and Karoui, 2018). Our analysis is based on delta-hedged holding-period returns. Specifically, on each portfolio formation date, we buy one call option contract and sell ∆ shares of the underlying stock, where ∆ is from OptionMetrics and is calculated based on the Black-Scholes model. We maintain the position for one month without daily rebalancing. This follows the monthly buy-andhold delta-hedged return constructions commonly used in the literature in order to limit transaction costs (see, e.g., Goyal and Saretto, 2009;Bali and Murray, 2013;Zhan, Han, Cao, and Tong, 2022). 6 The delta-hedged option return is then defined as

Estimating the conditional factor model in (2.5) using the regressed-PCA approach yields a set of factors that capture common variation across stock, corporate bond, and option markets. Figure 1 plots the cumulative returns of the first five common factors. Several factors exhibit strong systematic fluctuations during major episodes in financial markets, indicating that these factors are able to capture the common sources of aggregate risk. In this section, we examine the cross-market commonality captured by the extracted factors and interpret their underlying economic driving forces.

We investigate the commonality captured by the factors from several aspects. We compare them with the observable factors in each asset class. We relate the common factors to the latent factors extracted from individual asset markets via regressed-PCA, and further analyze the contributions of their components from different asset classes.

We begin by examining the connection between the common factors and observable factors, which have been widely adopted in the literature and shown to explain substantial crosssectional return variation within each asset class. For stocks, we follow Fama and French (2015) and Carhart (1997) and choose the market factor (M KT stock), size (SM B), value (HM L), profitability (RM W ), investment (CM A), and momentum (M OM ). For corporate bonds, following Bai, Bali, and Wen (2019) and Dickerson, Mueller, and Robotti (2023), we select bond market factor (M KT bond), credit risk (CRF ), liquidity risk (LRF ), bond momentum (M OM B), bond return reversal (REV ), and long-term reversal (LT R). For options, we use factors from Goyal and Saretto (2009), Zhan, Han, Cao, and Tong (2022), and Büchner and Kelly (2022): volatility level (LEV EL), moneyness skewness (SKEW ), idiosyncratic volatility (IV OL), illiquidity (ILQ), option-market factor (M KT option), and volatility deviation (V OLDEV ). More details on the observable factors are provided in Appendix A2. Table 2 shows the time-series regression results of each common factor on observable factors. Most common factors are significantly explained by observable factors from different asset classes. For example, the first factor loads positively on SMB and RMW, which largely absorb its positive univariate correlations with the equity market portfolio and HML, and negatively on the stock MOM factor. This is consistent with findings that value and momentum factors are negatively correlated (see, e.g., Asness, Moskowitz, and Pedersen, 2013), and that HML is largely absorbed when RMW and CMA are controlled for (see, e.g., Fama and French, 2015). It also loads significantly on the credit risk and liquidity risk factors (see, e.g., Dickerson, Mueller, and Robotti, 2023). The observable factors explain a substantial proportion of the variation in our common factors, with adjusted R 2 ranging from 19% to 57%. 7 The high R 2 and correlations indicate that the extracted factors, as established observable factors, effectively capture substantial cross-sectional common variation across different asset classes. However, almost all of the common factors carry positive risk premia beyond those captured by the observable factors, as reflected in significantly positive intercepts. This finding suggests that common factors built from the bottom up capture systematic risks that are not fully spanned by the top-down factors, which are built to exploit the predictive power of characteristics for asset returns.

To understand the economic meaning of the common factors, we explore their relations with a broad set of macroeconomic and financial variables, which are key indicators of the financial market conditions. We group these variables into three categories: economic activity indicators, including core inflation, consumption growth (c), and growth in industrial production (IP); uncertainty measures, including economic policy uncertainty (EPU) from Baker, Bloom, and Davis (2016), financial uncertainty (FINU) and macro uncertainty (MACU) from Jurado, Ludvigson, and Ng (2015); financial conditions, including federal funds rate (FFR), term spread (TERM), credit spread (DEF), VIX index, intermediary capital factor (HKM) from He, Kelly, and Manela (2017), and the liquidity factor from Pástor and Stambaugh (2003). Certain series are first-differenced, denoted by ∆p¨q, to ensure stationarity. We examine the economic linkage from two perspectives. First, we assess the relation of macro-financial variables with the common factors and analyze the explanatory contribution of each asset-class-specific component. Second, we use the common factors to predict macrofinancial variables. We find that the common factors have strong predictive power over the macro-financial variables, reflecting their tight relevance to the underlying state of the aggregate economy.

Table 5 reports the pairwise correlations between common factors and macro-financial variables, showing the strong correlations between them. In detail, the first common factor is significantly associated with financial market and economic conditions: it is negatively correlated with the credit spreads, uncertainty indices and the VIX, and positively correlated with the term spreads and the intermediary capital (HKM) factor. Consistent with Figure 2, this finding implies that the first factor is cyclical. The second factor is sensitive to monetary conditions. It negatively correlates with inflation and the federal funds rate, indicating that a tightening monetary shock is associated with a decline in factor returns. In addition, this factor is negatively correlated with VIX and financial uncertainty. The third common factor shows strong and positive associations with core inflation, consumption growth, and industrial production growth, suggesting that it co-moves significantly with macroeconomic fundamentals. Given the strong common factor structure across markets documented in the previous sections, a natural question arises: does the strong cross-market commonality reflect a high degree of market integration? On the one hand, we observe substantial comovement among asset returns across markets over time, as captured by the common factors. On the other hand, the high Sharpe ratio of the joint MVE portfolio that exploits commonality in asset returns by taking opposite positions on the same factors in different asset classes might potentially reflect relative mispricing of the common factors across markets. If the same factor exposures earn different prices of risk in different markets, which could arise if markets were segmented, these price dispersions might be behind the evidence of cross-market hedging documented in Section 6. In this section, we develop a formal statistical test that allows us to gauge the degree of cross-market segmentation. Is this evidence of market segmentation related to the finding of cross-market hedging documented in Section 6? In Table 14, we use the characteristic-managed portfolios ( r R X ) to construct the joint and single-market MVE portfolios and SDFs, and report their weights on common factors as well as the implied common factor risk premia in different markets. We find that cross-market hedging is mainly reflected in the different risk premia earned by the same factors in different markets, that is, the joint MVE portfolio tends to take a long (short) position on a common factor in the market where the factor earns a higher (lower) risk premium. For instance, the implied risk premium of the second common factor in the option market is the largest across the three markets (4.78, compared to 2.52 in stocks and 0.56 in bonds), so that the corresponding option component takes the largest long position (2.75); the stock component has a smaller long position (1.10), while the corporate bond component takes a short position (-1.47) on this factor with the smallest risk premium. By contrast, all single-market MVE portfolios have positive weights on the second common factor (1.13, 0.25, and 2.13 in stocks, bonds, and options, respectively). In addition, we report estimates of factor risk premia implied by the joint SDF constructed across the managed portfolio spaces ( λJ ). The results provide further evidence of the failure of cross-market LOOP or market segmentation, since the null of market integration implies that common factor risk premia according to a "joint" or any single-market SDF should be identical. This is clearly not the case for most factors, implying that the same common payoffs are priced differently in these markets.

Since common factors are the basis of the common payoff space, a mean-variance investor would allocate more capital to the markets with higher common factor risk premia, and short the common factors in the market with the lowest prices of risk, exploiting the price differences and then hedging some of the common factor exposure to reduce portfolio volatility. As a result, the joint MVE portfolio features insignificant exposures to most of the common factors as shown in Tables 11 and 14, although these factors earn substantially positive Sharpe ratios shown in Table 8. Overall, uncovering common factors leads us to conclude that asset market segmentation might be behind the high Sharpe ratios earned by crossmarket MVE portfolios, as statistically significant differences between factors' risk prices in different markets are largely behind the observed cross-market hedging, which results in small exposures of the cross-market MVE portfolios to the common factors.

In this paper, we identify a strong common factor structure across major corporate securities: stocks, corporate bonds, and options. We extract common factors jointly from individual asset returns via the regressed-PCA in a conditional factor model across three asset markets. Common factors effectively capture systematic sources of risk that affect returns of corporate securities, and reveal additional information about the state of the aggregate economy. The factors account for substantial variation in asset returns both in-sample and out-ofsample, while the presence of mispricing that can be exploited to construct "arbitrage" portfolios points to meaningful deviations from APT-type factor pricing. We demonstrate how to build a joint MVE portfolio using a large cross-section of individual assets by relying on a smaller set of characteristic-managed portfolios or common factors. The joint MVE portfolio achieves a high Sharpe ratio in large part due to crossmarket hedging, whereby its common factor exposures are effectively neutralized by taking opposite exposures on the factors in different asset classes. This is true not just in-sample but also, to a large degree, out-of-sample. Common factors can be used as the benchmark basis payoffs in order to gauge the extent of market integration, which is reflected in heterogeneous risk premia earned by the common factors across markets. Our analysis reveals significant segmentation between all market pairs, but especially those involving options. Our formal statistical tests of market integration support the argument that the cross-market hedging of common factors exhibited by our MVE portfolios is largely caused by differences in risk premia associated with the same factors.

Our results open promising directions for future research. We show how to construct common factors that are capable of explaining substantial return variation both across and within asset classes. We also develop a novel approach to constructing MVE portfolios from individual assets that can be applied to other asset classes, including those with unbalanced panels and short return histories. Our proposed framework for measuring market segmentation is also applicable to broader contexts, such as international financial markets. Finally, our empirical finding of significant market segmentation also challenges the assumption of integrated asset markets, putting greater impetus on understanding market frictions and limits to arbitrage.
